title: Two calorimeters, one reaction - why a sealed bomb measures ΔU and a constant-pressure calorimeter measures ΔH
summary: The same fuel burns in a sealed bomb calorimeter (constant volume, no work: q_V = ΔU) and in an idealised constant-pressure piston calorimeter (q_p = ΔH). The heats differ by the expansion work, ΔH − ΔU = Δn_g RT, which vanishes when the moles of gas do not change (graphite).
subject: Chemistry
subtopics: Bomb calorimeter: constant volume, q_V = ΔU
Expansion work at constant pressure: w = −pΔV = −Δn_g RT
Sign of q for an exothermic reaction from the calorimeter's temperature rise
concepts: A bolted bomb cannot change volume, so no work is done and all of ΔU appears as heat: q_V = ΔU
At constant pressure the gas volume follows the gas moles, the piston moves, and q_p = ΔU + pΔV = ΔH
ΔH − ΔU = Δn_g RT, counting only gaseous moles; Δn_g = 0 gives ΔH = ΔU (graphite)
The calorimeter gains the heat the reaction loses: q_reaction = −C_cal ΔT
learningObjectives: Explain why a bomb calorimeter measures the change in internal energy of a reaction.
Compare measurements at constant volume and at constant pressure, and the quantity each one gives.
Calculate the energy change of a reaction from the temperature change and heat capacity of a calorimeter.
Derive ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT for a reaction involving ideal gases.
Calculate ΔH from ΔU, or ΔU from ΔH, for a reaction or phase change involving gases.
Predict whether ΔH and ΔU differ significantly for a reaction, from the change in moles of gas.
Predict the sign of ΔH for a reaction that evolves or absorbs heat at constant pressure.
